legend.name: Light moth
legend.meaning: Pale with dark speckles (speckles not shown)

steps.title: Pale trunk
steps.instruction: Trace the tree trunk on the left.

note.text: In clean air, tree bark is covered in pale lichen. This was normal in England before the 1800s.

steps.title: Dark trunk
steps.instruction: Trace the tree trunk on the right.

note.text: Factory smoke in the 1800s killed the lichen and coated bark in black soot.

steps.title: Light moths
steps.instruction: Trace a light moth on each tree.

note.text: Most peppered moths were pale and speckled, a perfect match for lichen-covered bark.
note.remember: Camouflage: blending in to stay hidden.

steps.title: Dark moths
steps.instruction: Trace a dark moth on each tree.

note.text: A few peppered moths are born dark. On pale bark, birds spot and eat them easily.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: Color the trees and moths, then look at which moths are easy to see.

steps.title: Spot the moth
steps.question: On the dark, sooty tree, which moth is a hungry bird more likely to catch?

options.feedback: Yes. It stands out against the dark bark, while the dark moth blends in.
The dark moth matches the sooty bark, so it's hidden. The light one stands out.
Look at the colors: one moth matches the bark and one doesn't.
Many birds eat moths. That's why camouflage matters.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: As the trees got darker, what happened to the moths over many years?

options.text: Dark moths became more common, because more of them survived to have young
options.feedback: Right. Dark moths survived better, so more young were dark. When the air was cleaned up, pale moths became common again.
A moth can't change its color. More dark moths survived and passed their color on.
The moths that matched the bark survived and kept the species going.
Scientists recorded a big change: dark moths went from rare to common.
